lessons.title: What is Physical AI?
lessons.body_html:
Robots, plus AI, plus operations

Physical AI is what happens when autonomous machines — here, AMRs (autonomous mobile robots) — do real work in real buildings, and software has to keep them productive, safe, and observable. It is not one thing but three layers stacked together: the robots themselves (navigation, batteries, motors, safety fields), the AI that assists the humans running them (an incident detector, predictive-maintenance trends, a fleet copilot), and the operations discipline that makes the whole thing trustworthy (alarm hygiene, human approval of commands, audit trails, incident review).

Hype versus reality

The hype says robots run themselves. The reality on any production floor is different, and this platform is honest about it:

  • Robots fault. In the bundled simulator, robot AMR-07 deterministically loses localization — the message reads: Localization lost: LiDAR scan does not match map. Real fleets see the same class of failure every week.
  • AI here is decision support, not decision making. The detector opens incidents automatically, but a human resolves the root cause. The copilot (Sarathi) answers questions with cited evidence — and when it has no LLM key it degrades to computed template answers rather than guessing.
  • Commands to robots pass through a human approval gate. Pause, resume, send-to-charge and e-stop are queued as pending rows and executed only after an operator approves — with a full audit of who asked and who decided.

The platform you will train on

YantraFleet is an end-to-end fleet-operations platform for multi-vendor AMR fleets. Robots (or the bundled deterministic simulator: 10 AMRs from 3 vendors on an 8x5 waypoint grid with chargers) speak VDA 5050 v2.1; everything lands in one shared backend with a small set of tables you will use throughout this course: robots, alerts, incidents, commands, missions, robot_telemetry, and maintenance_findings.

You can run the entire stack with zero cloud accounts: python -m yantraops up --loopback starts an embedded in-memory backend, the simulator, the incident detector, the notifier (in dry-run), the Sarathi copilot, and a live web console — all on localhost.

What good operators actually do

An operator's value is judgment under noise: knowing which of thirty alerts matters, whether a fault needs a technician or a re-init, when to pause a robot and when to leave it alone. This track teaches the exact vocabulary and workflows the platform enforces — canonical statuses, alarm acknowledgment, incident reading, and the command gate — so your judgment operates on precise, shared terms rather than vibes.
key_points: Physical AI = robots + AI decision support + operations discipline; none of the three works alone.
AI on this platform assists humans (detection, trends, grounded answers); it does not command robots autonomously.
All robot commands pass a human approval gate with a full audit trail.
The whole platform runs locally with one command: python -m yantraops up --loopback.
Seven backend tables carry everything: robots, alerts, incidents, commands, missions, robot_telemetry, maintenance_findings.
The simulator is deterministic — AMR-07 always loses localization, so training scenarios are repeatable.

quiz.q: On this platform, who ultimately executes a pause or e-stop command on a robot?
options: The AI copilot decides and executes autonomously
The command is queued and only executes after a human approves it
Commands execute immediately when any console button is clicked
Only the robot vendor's own software can command robots
quiz.explain: Robot actions queue as pending rows in the commands table; an operator approves or rejects each one, and only approved commands are executed. This human-in-the-loop gate is a core design principle.

quiz.q: What does the loopback demo (yantraops up --loopback) require you to set up first?
options: A Supabase cloud account and API keys
An MQTT broker on your network
Nothing — it runs an embedded in-memory backend with zero config
A physical robot connected over USB
quiz.explain: Loopback mode starts an embedded in-memory backend plus the simulator, detector, notifier, copilot, and console — no cloud, no keys, no robots.

quiz.q: Which statement best matches the honest reality of Physical AI operations?
options: Modern AMR fleets run unattended; operators are being phased out
AI predicts every fault before it happens, so incidents are rare
Robots fault regularly; AI helps humans detect, diagnose, and respond faster
Robots only fault when misconfigured by integrators
quiz.explain: Faults are routine (the simulator scripts one on AMR-07 on purpose). The platform's AI shortens detection and diagnosis; humans still own the response.

Start the full platform locally and see your fleet come alive.

  • Wait for the READY banner and open the console URL it prints.
  • Watch the live map for a minute: 10 simulated AMRs from 3 vendors picking, dropping, moving, and charging.

Verification passes once the simulator has written at least one robot row to the backend.

lessons.title: Reading a Fleet: Statuses, Battery, Health
lessons.body_html:
One vocabulary, everywhere

Early versions of this platform had three diverging status vocabularies (the simulator said working/moving/safety_stop, the connector said estop/active, the console said fault/paused). v0.2 fixed that at the source: every component now writes and reads exactly seven canonical statuses, and the database enforces it with a CHECK constraint. Learn them cold — they are the shared language of every alarm, incident, and shift handover:

  • active — doing useful work or driving to it
  • idle — powered, healthy, no task
  • charging — at a charger, charging
  • paused — deliberately held by an operator (resumable)
  • estop — emergency/safety stop (operator or safety field)
  • degraded — running, but with WARNING-level errors
  • fault — FATAL error; not operating

Two of these — fault and estop — count as not-operating for analytics and copilot purposes. Note the semantic difference between paused (a human chose this; it is safe and resumable) and estop (a safety event; treat with urgency). Legacy spellings like working, safety_stop, or offline are normalized on write; an unknown status becomes idle — readers never crash on a stranger's string.

The robot row

Each robot is one row in the robots table: id, vendor, status, battery (percent), pos (an [x, y] pair), speed, task_kind (pick, drop, move, inventory — or transit), health (a 0-100 heuristic), motor_temp, tasks_done, fault_msg, and updated_at. Reading a fleet means scanning these fields fast:

  • Battery: below 20 percent raises a warn alert; below 10 percent, crit. Robots route themselves to chargers, so a low battery on an active robot is normal — a low battery on an idle robot that never charges is not.
  • Health: a heuristic score docked for fatal errors, warnings, safety stops, and low battery. It is a triage aid, not a diagnosis.
  • fault_msg: when status is fault, this carries the first fatal error's description — read it before doing anything else.
  • updated_at: a stale timestamp means the robot (or its data path) went quiet — which is itself a finding.

Reading patterns, not snapshots

A single glance tells you little. Fleets breathe: robots cycle active, idle, and charging all day. What you are looking for is deviation — one robot charging far more often than its peers, a vendor's robots all degraded at once, speeds trending down. The console's live map updates continuously; make a habit of scanning status distribution first, then outliers.
key_points: Exactly seven canonical statuses: active, idle, charging, paused, estop, degraded, fault — enforced by a DB CHECK constraint.
paused means an operator deliberately held the robot (safe, resumable); estop is a safety event.
fault and estop are the two not-operating statuses; degraded means running with WARNING-level errors.
Battery alerts: warn at 20 percent or less, crit at 10 percent or less.
health is a 0-100 triage heuristic; fault_msg carries the first fatal error's description.
Read patterns and deviations, not snapshots — a stale updated_at is itself a signal.

quiz.q: A robot shows status degraded. What does that mean?
options: It is stopped with a fatal error
It is running, but with WARNING-level errors
An operator paused it
Its battery is below 10 percent
quiz.explain: degraded is the canonical status for a robot that keeps operating while carrying WARNING-level errors. Fatal errors produce fault, which stops operation.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between paused and estop?
options: They are synonyms in the canonical vocabulary
paused is set by the robot; estop is set by the console
paused is a deliberate, resumable operator hold; estop is an emergency/safety stop
estop robots keep moving slowly; paused robots stop
quiz.explain: paused means a human chose to hold the robot and it can be resumed; estop means an emergency or safety-field stop and is treated as not-operating, with urgency.

quiz.q: The connector receives a status string it has never seen. What happens?
options: The row is rejected by the database
The reader crashes with a validation error
It is normalized to idle — the least alarming guess
It is stored verbatim for later cleanup
quiz.explain: The canonical-status contract maps known legacy spellings to canon and turns anything unknown into idle, so no reader ever crashes on a stranger's status string, and the DB constraint is never violated.

quiz.q: At what battery levels do alerts fire?
options: warn at 50 percent, crit at 25 percent
warn at 20 percent or less, crit at 10 percent or less
A single crit alert at 5 percent
Battery never raises alerts; robots self-manage charging
quiz.explain: Low battery fires a warn alert at 20 percent or below and crit at 10 percent or below, with hysteresis (reset only above 25 percent) to prevent flapping.

practical.instructions_html:
With the loopback platform running, practice reading the fleet.

  • On the console's live map, identify one robot in each of at least three different statuses (for example active, idle, charging).
  • Open one robot's detail view and read its battery, health, motor temperature, and task.
  • Find a robot that is charging or heading to a charger, and note its battery percentage — is it consistent with the 20 percent warn threshold?

Verification passes once at least one charging sample exists in the telemetry history — which happens naturally as the simulated fleet cycles.

lessons.tutor_context: Lesson: Reading a fleet. Canonical status vocabulary (core/yantracore/status.py, enforced by DB CHECK in 0002_commands.sql): active (doing useful work or driving to it), idle (powered, healthy, no task), charging (at charger), paused (deliberately held by operator, resumable), estop (emergency/safety stop), degraded (running with WARNING-level errors), fault (FATAL error, not operating). NOT_OPERATING = {fault, estop}. Legacy map: working/moving/to_charger/driving -> active; safety_stop/estopped/e-stop -> estop; error/faulted/offline -> fault; unknown -> idle (readers never crash). robots row: id, vendor, status, battery (numeric percent), pos jsonb [x,y], speed, task_kind (pick/drop/move/inventory, or transit), health (0-100 heuristic: -40 per fatal, -10 per warning, -15 safety stop, -10 low battery), motor_temp, tasks_done, fault_msg (first fatal error description), updated_at, site_id. Battery alerts: warn at <=20 percent, crit at <=10 percent, resets only above 25 percent (5-point hysteresis, no flapping). Sim vendors: nexomotion, agilus, boturo; 10 robots; 8x5 waypoint grid with chargers. Teaching emphasis: paused vs estop distinction; degraded still operates; stale updated_at = data path or robot silent; read distributions and deviations, not snapshots.

lessons.title: Alarm Discipline
lessons.body_html:
Why alarm discipline exists

Industrial operations learned the hard way that alarm systems fail by succeeding too much: floods of low-value alarms train operators to ignore everything, including the one that matters. The process industry codified the answer in ISA-18.2 — alarm management as a lifecycle: every alarm must be meaningful, prioritized, acknowledged by a person, and rationalized over time. This platform applies that spirit to AMR fleets.

Severity tiers

Alerts in the alerts table carry a severity: info, warn, and crit from the simulator and connector (a fatal VDA error maps to crit, a WARNING-level error to warn), and incidents add a serious tier (e-stop conditions). Severity determines urgency of response and who gets notified: the notifier only pushes unacked crit and serious events to external channels. Everything else stays on the console — by design.

The ack workflow

Acknowledging an alert (ack flips from false to true) is a professional act with a precise meaning: a human has seen this and owns the response. It does not mean fixed. The workflow:

  • Triage by severity first, then by recency. Crit before warn, always.
  • Read the message and source. Every alert carries msg, src, and a time label.
  • Ack it — this stops repeated external notification and tells your teammates it is being handled.
  • Act or escalate. Ack without follow-through is worse than no ack: it silences the alarm while the condition persists.

Alarm budgets and dedup

The platform fights alarm floods at the source. The connector deduplicates: a VDA error raises exactly one alert on its inactive-to-active transition and stays silent while the error persists; when the error clears and later recurs, that is a genuinely new alert. Low-battery alerts use 5-point hysteresis — fire at 20 percent, reset only above 25 percent — so a battery hovering at the threshold cannot flap. Treat your remaining alert volume as a budget: if operators see more than a handful of crit alerts per shift, that is an engineering problem to fix (bad thresholds, a flapping robot, a missing dedup), not a fact of life to endure. Chronic unacked alerts are a red flag in either direction: real problems being ignored, or noise that should be rationalized away.

What ack is not

Ack is not resolution (incidents track that, next lesson), not silencing forever, and not a group activity — one person acks and owns. If you ack something you cannot handle, say so and hand it off explicitly.
key_points: ISA-18.2 spirit: every alarm should be meaningful, prioritized, acknowledged, and rationalized — floods destroy operator trust.
Severity tiers: info / warn / crit on alerts; incidents add serious (e-stop). Crit and serious drive external notification.
The notifier only pushes unacked crit/serious events — acking stops repeat notification.
Ack means a human has seen it and owns the response — not that it is fixed.
Dedup at the source: one alert per error activation edge; low-battery uses 5-point hysteresis (fire at 20, reset above 25).
Treat alert volume as a budget: chronic floods are an engineering defect to rationalize, not background noise.

quiz.q: What does acknowledging an alert mean on this platform?
options: The underlying condition is fixed
The alert was a false positive
A human has seen it and owns the response
The alert is deleted from the table
quiz.explain: Ack flips the ack flag to true: it signals ownership and stops repeat external notification. Resolution is tracked separately, on incidents.

quiz.q: Which events does the notifier push to external channels (webhook/WhatsApp)?
options: Every alert, regardless of severity
Only unacked crit and serious events, plus Open incidents
Only info alerts, to avoid alarm fatigue
Nothing — the notifier is console-only
quiz.explain: The notifier polls unacked crit/serious alerts and Open incidents, dedups per event, and fans out. Lower severities stay on the console by design — that is the alarm budget at work.

quiz.q: A robot's battery hovers around 20 percent for ten minutes. How many low-battery alerts fire?
options: One per state message — potentially dozens
One per minute
Exactly one, until battery recovers above 25 percent
None — battery alerts only fire below 10 percent
quiz.explain: Low-battery alerting uses 5-point hysteresis: it fires once at 20 percent or below and can only re-fire after recovery above 25 percent. This prevents threshold flapping.

quiz.q: Per ISA-18.2 thinking, a fleet where operators see hundreds of alarms per shift is:
options: Well-instrumented — more visibility is always better
An engineering defect: floods train operators to ignore the alarm that matters
Normal for any robot fleet over 5 robots
Only a problem if the alarms are crit severity
quiz.explain: Alarm floods destroy the signal value of every alarm. The fix is rationalization — better thresholds, dedup, and severity discipline — not operator endurance.

practical.instructions_html:
Work a live alert end to end.

  • With the loopback platform running, open the console's alerts view. Faults and low batteries in the simulated fleet generate alerts continuously.
  • Triage: find the highest-severity unacked alert. Read its message, source, and time label.
  • Acknowledge it from the console.
  • Say out loud (or write down) what your next action would be on a real floor: dispatch, monitor, or escalate.

Verification passes once at least one alert in the backend is acked.

lessons.tutor_context: Lesson: Alarm discipline, ISA-18.2 spirit (alarm lifecycle: meaningful, prioritized, acknowledged, rationalized; floods destroy trust). alerts table: id, sev, msg, src, tlabel, ack boolean (default false), created_at, site_id. Severities: sim emits info/warn/crit; connector maps VDA WARNING -> warn, FATAL -> crit (v3.0 CRITICAL/URGENT also -> crit); detector incidents use crit (fault) and serious (estop). Notifier (yantranotify): polls UNACKED crit/serious alerts + Open incidents every ~10s, dedups per event, fans out console/webhook (WEBHOOK_URL)/WhatsApp (Twilio env); channels without creds print payloads. Acking stops repeat notification. Dedup at source (yantrabridge AlertDeduper): alert fires only on inactive->active edge per (serial, errorType, errorLevel); persisting error silent; cleared-then-recurring = new alert with new id; deterministic ids + ignore-duplicates insert = retry-safe. Low battery: warn <=20, crit <=10, reset only above 25 (5-point hysteresis). Ack semantics: human owns response, NOT resolution (incidents track that), one owner, follow through or hand off explicitly. Alarm budget: crit alerts per shift should be countable on one hand; chronic floods = engineering defect to rationalize.

lessons.title: Incidents and Replay
lessons.body_html:
From alert to incident

Alerts are events; incidents are managed problems. The incident detector (yantradetect) polls the robots table on an interval (default 5 seconds) and opens an incident when a robot is seen in fault or estop for two consecutive polls — the pending window that filters out one-poll blips, in the spirit of how mature monitoring systems avoid paging on transients. Severity follows the condition: fault opens a crit incident, estop opens serious.

Reading an incident

An incident row carries: id (deterministic INC-style ids, so retried writes are idempotent), sev, title, src (the robot id), state (Open or Resolved), impact, dur (minutes), and two fields a human or copilot fills in afterward: rca (root-cause analysis) and fix. When the robot recovers, the detector resolves the incident automatically with its final duration and impact. Three behaviors matter for how you read them:

  • Re-open window: if the same robot goes bad again shortly after resolution, the existing incident re-opens rather than spawning a duplicate — with a flap counter. An incident marked flapping is telling you the fix did not hold.
  • Stale auto-resolve: incidents do not linger forever on dead data.
  • Idempotency: deterministic ids mean the detector can crash, restart, and re-seed from open incidents without double-counting.

Replay: see what the robot saw

Opening an incident in the console fetches the robot's robot_telemetry rows in a window around the incident's creation time and drives a replay: the map shows the robot's actual recorded path, a scrubber moves through time, and battery/speed charts render from real samples. Alerts inside the window appear as event dots on the timeline. This is the operator's flight recorder — you can watch the minutes before the fault: was the robot slowing down? Was motor temperature climbing? Did an obstacle alert precede the fault?

One honest caveat: with fewer than 10 recorded samples the console falls back to a scripted demo replay (INC-1042) and says so with a note. Know the difference between real replay and the demo.

RCA is a narrative, not a checkbox

A good RCA answers three questions: what happened (mechanism, not symptom), why it happened (the condition that allowed it), and what prevents recurrence. The fix field should be concrete enough that a flapping re-open would prove it wrong. When you review a resolved incident, read rca and fix critically — the flap counter is the system grading your team's fixes.
key_points: The detector opens an incident after a robot is in fault/estop for two consecutive polls — the pending window filters blips.
Severity mapping: fault opens crit, estop opens serious.
Incidents auto-resolve on recovery with duration and impact; rca and fix are filled in by humans or the copilot.
Re-open window + flap counting: a recurring incident re-opens (marked flapping) instead of duplicating — flapping means the fix did not hold.
Replay drives the map, scrubber, and battery/speed charts from real robot_telemetry samples around the incident; alerts become event dots.
Fewer than 10 recorded samples triggers the scripted INC-1042 demo replay, clearly noted — know real from demo.

quiz.q: Why does the detector wait for two consecutive polls before opening an incident?
options: The database is too slow for single-poll writes
It is a pending window that filters one-poll transients so blips do not open incidents
Two polls are needed to compute severity
The robot must confirm the fault itself
quiz.explain: A robot must be seen in fault/estop for 2 consecutive polls before an incident opens — the same flap-guard idea mature monitoring systems use to avoid paging on transients.

quiz.q: An incident's impact field reads flapping. What is the system telling you?
options: The robot's position sensor is oscillating
The incident re-opened repeatedly shortly after being resolved — the fix is not holding
The detector is misconfigured
Telemetry samples are arriving out of order
quiz.explain: The re-open window merges a quick recurrence into the same incident and increments a flap counter; past the threshold the incident is marked flapping. It is the system grading the durability of your fixes.

quiz.q: What data drives the console's incident replay?
options: A physics re-simulation of the fleet
The robot's recorded robot_telemetry rows in a window around the incident, with alerts as event dots
Live current positions of all robots
The incident's rca text, rendered as an animation
quiz.explain: Replay fetches real recorded telemetry around the incident's created_at and drives the map, scrubber, and battery/speed charts from those samples. Under 10 samples, a clearly-noted scripted demo (INC-1042) is shown instead.

practical.instructions_html:
Read a real incident end to end.

  • With the loopback platform running, wait for the simulated fleet to fault (AMR-07's scripted localization fault guarantees at least one incident early in the run).
  • Open the console's incidents view and open the most recent incident.
  • Identify: the source robot, severity, state, and duration. If it resolved, read how long it lasted.
  • Run the replay: scrub through the timeline and watch the battery/speed charts. Note whether you are seeing real telemetry or the demo fallback (the console tells you).

Verification passes once the detector has written at least one incident.

lessons.tutor_context: Lesson: Incidents and replay. Detector (yantradetect): polls robots every N s (default 5; also --once/--dry-run), opens incident when robot in fault/estop for 2 consecutive polls (pending window, flap guard). Severity: fault -> crit, estop -> serious. Incident row: id (deterministic INC-XXXX, idempotent retried writes), sev, title, src = robot id, tlabel, state Open/Resolved, impact, rca, fix (nullable, patched by console/copilot), dur (minutes), created_at, site_id. Auto-resolve on recovery with duration+impact; stale auto-resolve; restart re-seeds from GET incidents?state=eq.Open. Re-open window: same robot bad again shortly after resolution re-opens the SAME incident, flap_count increments; past flap_threshold, impact gains flapping marker — signals fix did not hold. Replay: console fetches robot_telemetry rows in window around incident created_at; drives map path, scrubber, battery/speed charts; alerts in window = event dots. Fewer than 10 samples -> scripted INC-1042 demo replay with a note. robot_telemetry: ~1 sample/robot per ~6s sim time, 72h retention via purge_old_telemetry(). RCA guidance: mechanism, enabling condition, prevention; fix should be falsifiable by a flap. Scripted AMR-07 localization fault (tick 20, 12 ticks) guarantees a teachable incident.

lessons.title: The Command Gate: Human-in-the-Loop Control
lessons.body_html:
Why a gate at all

Software that can move multi-hundred-kilogram machines around a building shared with people should not act on a single click — or on an AI's judgment. The command gate turns every robot action into a two-step, two-human-capable workflow: someone requests, someone approves, and everything is recorded. This is deliberate friction. It converts what would be an instantaneous, unaccountable action into an auditable decision.

The four verbs

The platform supports exactly four commands, matching a CHECK constraint in the database: pause (hold the robot; resumable), resume (release a pause), charge (send to a charger), and estop (emergency stop). That small vocabulary is a feature: every operator on every shift knows the complete action space.

Life of a command

When you click pause on a robot in the console (with a live backend connected), nothing happens to the robot yet. Instead a row is inserted into the commands table with status=pending, recording robot_id, cmd, and requested_by. Then:

  • The Pending approvals card on the console's Overview lists it. An operator approves or rejects; the row moves to approved or rejected, stamping decided_by and decided_at.
  • The executor — the running simulator, or a live robot bridge — polls for approved commands, applies them in the world, and marks each executed or failed, with a reason in note.
  • The full lifecycle is therefore: pending, then approved or rejected, then executed or failed. There is deliberately no intermediate sent state — a published-but-unconfirmed command stays approved and is deduplicated in memory so it is never re-sent.

Approve/reject is a responsibility

When you approve, you are the accountable human. Before approving, check: is the robot's current status consistent with the command (pausing a robot already in fault does little; resuming an estopped robot is not what resume is for)? Is there a reason someone requested this? Rejection is not rude — it is the gate doing its job; use note to say why. Never approve what you do not understand.

The audit trail

Every command row permanently records who asked (requested_by), who decided (decided_by), when (created_at, decided_at, executed_at), the outcome, and a free-text note. In a real deployment this is your answer to the question every safety review asks: who told the robot to do that, and on whose authority? On live MQTT fleets there is one honest caveat: commands are published once; a command sent while the robot is offline is lost and needs a fresh request and approval — the table will show it stuck at approved.
key_points: Four command verbs only: pause, resume, charge, estop — enforced by a DB CHECK constraint.
Console actions insert pending rows; nothing touches the robot until a human approves.
Lifecycle: pending -> approved/rejected -> executed/failed. No intermediate sent state, by design.
The executor (simulator or robot bridge) polls approved commands, applies them, and records executed/failed with a note.
Approving makes you the accountable human — verify status and intent first; reject with a note when unsure.
Full audit per command: requested_by, decided_by, created/decided/executed timestamps, outcome, note.

quiz.q: You click pause on a robot in the console (live backend connected). What happens immediately?
options: The robot pauses within one control cycle
A pending row is inserted into the commands table; the robot is untouched until approval
The copilot evaluates the request and decides
The robot pauses only if its battery is low
quiz.explain: Console actions queue as pending command rows. Only after a human approves does the executor apply the command in the world. That two-step flow is the human-in-the-loop gate.

quiz.q: Which is the complete, valid status lifecycle of a command row?
options: queued -> sent -> done
pending -> approved or rejected -> executed or failed
pending -> executing -> archived
requested -> validated -> committed
quiz.explain: Commands start pending; a human moves them to approved or rejected; the executor then marks approved commands executed or failed. There is deliberately no sent state.

quiz.q: Why does the audit trail record both requested_by and decided_by?
options: For load-balancing across operators
So safety reviews can answer who asked for the action and who authorized it
Because the database requires two non-null columns
To compute operator performance bonuses
quiz.explain: Separating requester from approver is the core of accountable control: any action on a robot can be traced to the human who requested it and the human who authorized it, with timestamps and outcome.

quiz.q: On a live MQTT fleet, a command is approved while the robot is offline. What does the table show?
options: The command retries forever until the robot returns
The command auto-fails after 60 seconds
The command stays approved; it was published once and lost, so a human must re-request and re-approve
The command is silently deleted
quiz.explain: Instant actions are published exactly once; a command published to an offline robot is lost and the row remains approved. The documented remedy is a fresh row through the gate — not silent retry.

practical.instructions_html:
Run a command through the full gate.

  • With the loopback platform running, open a robot's detail view in the console and request a pause.
  • Go to the Pending approvals card on Overview. Find your command; note who requested it.

lessons.title: VDA 5050 and Interoperability
lessons.body_html:
Why standards kill lock-in

Without a standard, every robot vendor ships its own fleet manager, and a warehouse running three vendors runs three control rooms. VDA 5050 — a standard from the German automotive industry association, spoken over MQTT — defines a common interface between AGVs/AMRs and a master controller. Any robot that speaks it can join any compliant fleet system. This platform is built on VDA 5050 v2.1: the simulator emits it, the connector consumes it, and a real robot that speaks it needs no custom code to appear on your console.

The topic scheme

VDA 5050 messages travel on MQTT topics of the form interfaceName/majorVersion/manufacturer/serialNumber/topic — concretely, uagv/v2/<manufacturer>/<serialNumber>/state for telemetry and .../instantActions for immediate commands. Serial numbers are sanitized to the allowed character set, so robot AMR-07 appears on the wire as AMR_07 while the database keeps AMR-07. The connection topic carries ONLINE/OFFLINE presence.

The state message

The state message is the robot's periodic self-report, and the connector's translation of it is worth knowing precisely:

  • batteryState.batteryCharge becomes battery; agvPosition becomes pos; speed is computed from the velocity vector.
  • Status is derived by priority: a FATAL error means fault; an e-stop or field violation means estop; charging, paused, driving, idle follow.
  • errors[] entries become alerts (WARNING maps to warn, FATAL to crit), deduplicated on activation edges.
  • Fields outside core VDA 5050 — motor temperature, tasks done — are passed through only when a vendor extends the payload; otherwise the columns are omitted so an upsert never clobbers another writer's values.

instantActions: commands going the other way

Approved commands flow back as instantActions: the bridge publishes actionType yantra.<cmd> with the command's uuid as actionId and blockingType HARD. The robot reports an actionStates entry (FINISHED or FAILED with a result description) in its next state messages, which closes the loop and marks the command row executed or failed. One standard, both directions.

What interop buys you

As a fleet admin, VDA 5050 means: one console and one alarm pipeline across vendors; the freedom to buy your next robots from a different vendor without replatforming; and replayable, vendor-neutral recordings. The platform's three simulated vendors (nexomotion, agilus, boturo) exist precisely to prove the multi-vendor path — the connector cannot tell them apart, and neither should your operations.

When you evaluate a new robot vendor, make VDA 5050 v2.1 compliance a line item in the RFP, and prove it cheaply: capture a few of their state messages and replay them through the connector's dry-run before any hardware ships. Ten minutes of replay tells you more than a hundred pages of datasheet.

lessons.title: Telemetry and Predictive Maintenance
lessons.body_html:
History is a table

Live status tells you what is; history tells you what is coming. Every writer downsamples robot state into robot_telemetry — roughly one sample per robot every six seconds of sim time — each row carrying robot_id, ts, battery, speed, motor_temp, status, and pos. A purge function keeps 72 hours of raw history, a deliberate free-tier discipline: enough for incident replay and trend detection, small enough to stay cheap. This same table powers the incident replay you met in the Operator track.

From history to findings

Run the detector in maintenance mode — python -m yantradetect --maintenance (optionally --window-hours 6) — and it reads recent telemetry windows and maintains the maintenance_findings table. Three specific, documented trend rules produce findings:

  • Drive motor: motor-temperature trend of at least 1.5 degrees C per hour, with a regression fit of r-squared at least 0.5 — a real trend, not noise.
  • Battery: drain at least 1.5 times the fleet median per active-minute — the robot is an outlier against its own peers, which self-adjusts as the fleet ages.
  • Drivetrain: active-speed decline of at least 15 percent across the window.

Reading a finding

Each finding row carries a human-readable finding description, a heuristic rul_days (remaining useful life), a confidence between 0 and 1, and a recommended action. Two invariants keep the table trustworthy: at most one Open finding exists per robot-plus-component, and findings are Cleared — never deleted — when the trend abates, so the history of near-misses survives. IDs are deterministic, so retried writes cannot duplicate.

Acting on findings

Treat rul_days and confidence as scheduling inputs, not verdicts. A drive-motor finding with high confidence and short RUL should move a robot into the next maintenance window; a low-confidence battery finding earns a watch, not a work order. The right habit is triage by (confidence, rul_days), then verify against raw telemetry — open the robot's history and look at the actual motor-temp curve before spending a technician's afternoon. A finding that clears on its own is still information: it goes to Cleared, and a robot that repeatedly generates-then-clears the same finding deserves a closer look.

Honest limits

These are heuristics over a 72-hour window, not survival models trained on your fleet. They will miss failure modes that do not show up in temperature, drain, or speed, and rul_days is an order-of-magnitude aid. Their value is earlier, cheaper attention — the difference between a scheduled swap and a mission-hour lost to a seized drivetrain.

lessons.title: Missions, Throughput, and Fleet KPIs
lessons.body_html:
Missions: work in fleet-sized units

Individual robot tasks (pick, drop, move, inventory) are too granular to manage a business on. Missions group them: a mission is a named batch of work assigned to a group of robots — think Outbound wave #1 or Cycle count — Storage A. On this platform the simulator keeps up to three missions in flight at once, each with two to four robots and ten to twenty planned tasks. A mission's row in the missions table carries its name, its robots list, a state that runs Queued to Running to Done, an integer prog percent, and a clock ETA. Robots' completed tasks credit their mission; every tick the snapshot is upserted idempotently, and the console's Missions view polls the table live and can insert new missions.

The KPIs that matter

As fleet admin, three families of numbers turn robot activity into business language:

  • Throughput — tasks completed per unit time (the fleet_meta heartbeat row tracks a throughput figure, and per-robot tasks_done accumulates). Missions give throughput a shape: waves per shift, progress percent against ETA.
  • Availability — the fraction of time robots are able to work. In canonical-status terms: not fault, not estop (the two not-operating statuses). Charging is a nuance — it is unavailable for tasks but healthy; separate scheduled charging from unplanned downtime in your reporting.
  • MTTR — mean time to repair/recover. Every incident records its duration in minutes (dur), so MTTR is computable directly from resolved incidents. The re-open flap counter keeps this honest: an incident that resolves and re-opens is not two fast recoveries, it is one bad fix.

SLAs: promises with instrumentation

An SLA is only meaningful when the platform can measure it. Useful fleet SLAs here: mission on-time completion (ETA vs actual), incident response (time from incident open to ack/first action), MTTR ceilings by severity (crit incidents resolved within N minutes), and availability floors per site. Every one of these is computable from tables you already know: missions, incidents, alerts, robots.

Reading throughput problems

When throughput drops, work the chain in order: are robots unavailable (check status distribution — faults? a charging pileup?), are they slow (speed trends in telemetry — drivetrain findings?), or is work starved (missions Queued but robots idle — an assignment problem, not a robot problem)? The platform separates these signals precisely so you do not guess: status tells availability, telemetry tells speed, missions tell work supply. Most throughput mysteries dissolve into one of the three.

lessons.title: Multi-Site and Security Posture
lessons.body_html:
One backend, many buildings

Every operational table carries a site_id column so one backend can host several facilities. The default is BLR-DC1 — the original deployment — and writers stamp their rows via a shared helper that reads the YANTRA_SITE_ID environment variable, falling back to the default. Two consequences worth internalizing: legacy writers that never heard of sites keep working (the column default fills in), and readers must treat site_id as optional on rows they consume. Hot read paths are indexed site-first, then by time — filtering by site is the intended access pattern.

Demo mode: open on purpose

Out of the box the platform is demo-open: a policy called demo_all lets anyone holding the anon (publishable) key read and write every table. That is a feature for evaluation — zero setup, throwaway data — and a liability for anything real. Know your key classes:

  • Publishable/anon key — designed to ship in browsers and client code. It is exactly as dangerous as your row-level security policies allow: fully open in demo mode, nothing at all in hardened mode.
  • service_role key — bypasses row-level security entirely. It is a server-side admin credential. Never ship it to a browser, embed it in the console, commit it to git, or put it in client-side code. Servers and cron jobs only.

Hardening: the 0006 migration

The hardening migration (supabase/0006_harden.sql, opt-in, idempotent) drops demo_all on every table and creates read-only access for the authenticated role. No write policy is created because none is needed — writers switch to the service_role key, which bypasses RLS. The anon key is left with no access at all. Immediately after running it: switch every writer's SUPABASE_KEY to the service_role key; set SARATHI_TOKEN (the copilot then requires a bearer token on its ask endpoint) and YANTRA_WEBHOOK_SECRET (the notifier then signs every webhook POST with an HMAC-SHA256 signature header receivers can verify); and decide the console story.

The console decision

The browser console has no login flow yet, so in hardened mode it goes dark. Two documented options: add Supabase Auth (preferred, planned), or grant anon read-only access — keeping the console loginless but harmless, since writes still require service_role. Read-only anon is fine for dashboards on trusted networks and wrong for sensitive data. Command approvals always need a server-side path in hardened mode: anon and authenticated deliberately have no write policy.

Where multi-site meets security

Today all sites share one open (or one hardened) policy set. The documented future path is per-site JWTs carrying a site claim, with per-table policies matching rows to the caller's site — plus a fleet-wide operator role for cross-site reads. Design your site_id hygiene now; tenancy enforcement builds on it later.

lessons.title: Architecture Tour
lessons.body_html:
The shape of the system

YantraFleet is a small constellation of independent processes that share exactly one thing: the backend schema. No component calls another directly — everything coordinates through tables over PostgREST. That single design decision is why you can kill, restart, replace, or add components without renegotiating interfaces. The modules:

  • sim/ (yantrasim) — deterministic 10-AMR warehouse simulator: 3 vendors, an 8x5 waypoint grid, chargers, random and scripted faults. Emits VDA 5050 v2.1 state; publishes to the backend directly, to MQTT, or to stdout.
  • connector/ (yantrabridge) — pure VDA 5050-to-rows translation, alert dedup, and a batched sink. Sources: JSONL replay or live MQTT. Also home to the MCAP importer and the command publisher.
  • detector/ (yantradetect) — polls robots and maintains incidents (pending window, deterministic ids, re-open/flap logic); in maintenance mode it reads telemetry windows and maintains findings instead.
  • notifier/ (yantranotify) — polls unacked crit/serious alerts and Open incidents, dedups, fans out to console/webhook/WhatsApp; credential-less channels print instead of sending.
  • copilot/ (sarathi) — a FastAPI service answering fleet questions with cited evidence, degrading through tiers; also exposes the same toolbox over MCP for external agents.
  • console/ — a single-file web console with no build step: live map, robot detail, alerts, incidents with replay, missions, the approval gate, and a copilot panel.
  • core/ (yantracore) — the canonical status contract and the site-id helper every component shares.
  • ops/ (yantraops) — the orchestrator: one command brings the stack up in loopback, cloud, or MQTT mode; plus migrate, doctor, and status.

The loopback trick

In loopback mode the orchestrator starts an in-process fake PostgREST on localhost first, then points every child at it via environment variables. The children cannot tell the difference — same HTTP, same filters, same rows. This is also how the offline end-to-end suite works: real localhost HTTP, zero network egress.

Coordination without a coordinator

Two patterns do the coordinating. First, writer election: the fleet_meta heartbeat row (id 1) carries a writer_id; a live simulator feed outranks console tabs, and consoles automatically become viewers while a simulator (or a future robot adapter) is publishing. Second, idempotent writes everywhere: deterministic incident and finding ids, upserts with conflict targets, duplicate-ignoring alert inserts — so any component can crash and retry without corrupting shared state.

Why this matters to integrators

Your integration surface is the schema, not any process's internals. Anything that can write well-formed rows is a first-class citizen — which is exactly how real robots join in the next lesson.
key_points: Components never call each other — all coordination flows through shared tables over PostgREST.

lessons.title: Connecting Real Robots
lessons.body_html:
Three on-ramps

A real robot joins the platform three ways, in increasing order of liveness: replay a recording file, import a robot bag, or bridge a live MQTT broker. All three go through the same connector and the same translation code, so what you validate offline holds online.

Live MQTT: the production path

Point the bridge at your broker: python -m yantrabridge --mqtt-host broker.local --mqtt-port 1883. It subscribes to the VDA state topics (by default uagv/v2/+/+/state) and translates every state message into robots rows, alerts, and a connector heartbeat. Any robot publishing compliant VDA 5050 v2.1 state — or any vendor adapter that emits it — appears on the console with no further code. Authentication flags cover username/password brokers; environment variables point at your backend.

Closing the loop: the commands flag

Add --commands (live MQTT mode only) and the bridge also runs the operator-command loop: it polls approved rows from the commands table, publishes each exactly once as an instantActions message on the robot's own topic, then watches the state messages it is already consuming for matching actionStates entries and PATCHes each command to executed or failed with the robot's result description. This is the same approval gate operators learned, now driving real hardware. Remember the documented caveat: publish-once semantics mean a command sent to an offline robot is lost until a human re-approves a fresh one — nothing silently retries into a machine that just came back.

Bring your own recording: MCAP import

Most robots can already give you an MCAP file — a ROS 2 rosbag with JSON-encoded topics, a Foxglove recording, anything writing raw JSON channels. The importer needs no ROS installation:

  • python -m yantrabridge import --mcap run.mcap --dry-run — inspect first: topics found, message counts, time range, rows that would be written. No network.
  • Bulk import writes one telemetry row per message with the original recording timestamps preserved, plus a final robots state and alerts from errors — instant historical fleet data.
  • --rate 4 replays at 4x real time, updating the robots table live so the console animates the recording.

Non-VDA robots: the topic map

Topics that look like VDA 5050 state are auto-detected and go through the standard translation. Everything else is skipped — unless you map it. A topic-map JSON file maps arbitrary topic patterns and payload fields to fleet columns: robot id from a topic segment, battery from a nested payload field, a status map translating vendor mode strings into the canonical vocabulary. With a dozen lines of JSON, a proprietary robot's recording becomes standard fleet history — no code.

Integration discipline

Always dry-run first — both the file replay and the importer support it. Validate the translated rows against what you know about the robot. Then go live, and watch the console with your own eyes before trusting the pipeline unattended.
key_points: Three on-ramps, one translation path: JSONL replay, MCAP import, live MQTT bridge.
Live bridge: yantrabridge --mqtt-host subscribes to uagv/v2/+/+/state; compliant VDA 5050 robots need zero custom code.
--commands adds the approved-command loop: publish instantActions once, close via actionStates, PATCH executed/failed.

The instantActions topics

File replay is too slow for commands

quiz.explain: The command publisher needs to publish to robot topics and observe returning actionStates in live state traffic; neither exists when replaying a file.

options: Convert it to CSV
Run the import with --dry-run to inspect topics, counts, time range, and the rows that would be written

quiz.explain: Dry-run inspection costs nothing (no network) and shows exactly what the importer detected and would write. No ROS installation is needed at any point — the importer reads MCAP directly.

options: You must write a custom Python translator
Rename the topics to VDA form in the robot firmware

It cannot be imported — only VDA 5050 sources are supported
quiz.explain: The --topic-map option maps arbitrary topics/fields to robot_id, battery, position, speed, status and more, including a status_map (e.g. MOVING to active, DOCKED to charging). No code required.

  • Replay the bundled recording through the full translation: python -m yantrabridge --file connector/sample.jsonl --dry-run, and confirm the three robots and their derived statuses.
  • Read the topic-map example in connector/README.md and sketch (on paper or in a scratch file) the map you would write for one of your own robots: which topic pattern, which payload field per column, and the status_map into the canonical vocabulary.
  • Identify the caveat you would brief operators on before enabling --commands on a live broker.

lessons.title: Copilots and Grounding
lessons.body_html:
A copilot you can audit

Sarathi, the fleet copilot, answers questions about your fleet — but the interesting part is how it earns trust. Every answer is built from a toolbox of live-data queries (fleet summary, robots, alerts, incidents, commands, robot history, telemetry), and each tool result carries a citation key. Answers cite their evidence; a claim without a source is a defect, not a style choice.

Three tiers, honest degradation

The service always answers, but it always tells you how much to trust the answer, via a tier label:

  • grounded — an LLM runs an agent loop over the live tools. Requires both an API key and a reachable data backend. This is the full experience: natural-language answers backed by fresh rows.
  • llm_only — the data backend is down but an LLM is available. The model answers from general knowledge, clearly labeled as not backed by live data.
  • offline — no LLM at all (no key, or the LLM failed). The service computes template answers directly from tool data. Less fluent, but grounded by construction.

The endpoint returns success with a tier field in every case — clients render the tier, and operators learn to read it. Degradation is a feature: a copilot that fails closed into silence is useless during an outage, and one that fails open into confident guessing is dangerous.

The grounding guard

LLMs sometimes emit numbers their evidence does not support. Sarathi runs a post-hoc guard on LLM-tier answers: it extracts the numeric tokens from the final text — deliberately skipping timestamps, clock times, entity-style ids like AMR-07 or INC-2, and evidence references, none of which are figures a model could meaningfully hallucinate — and requires each remaining number to appear in the tool-result payloads backing the answer. Formatting differences are tolerated (8 and 8.0 match; a payload value of 54.16 supports a quoted 54.2, since models legitimately round). The answer is then labeled verified or unverified, with offending tokens listed; offline-tier answers are labeled computed, being grounded by construction. An unverified label does not delete the answer — it tells the human exactly which claims to double-check.

Beyond the chat panel

The console's copilot panel calls the service with a short timeout and quietly falls back to a built-in rule engine when the service is not running — the UI never hangs on an LLM. And the same evidence-grounded toolbox is exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so external agents (a desktop assistant, another automation) can query your fleet through the identical tools, with the identical citations. One toolbox, many surfaces.

The integrator's takeaway

When you extend the copilot, preserve the contract: every capability is a tool that returns citable data, every answer declares its tier, and every number must trace to evidence. Fluency is optional; auditability is not.
key_points: Sarathi answers from a live-data toolbox (fleet summary, robots, alerts, incidents, commands, history, telemetry), with citation keys on every tool result.
Three tiers, always labeled: grounded (LLM + live tools) -> llm_only (LLM, backend down) -> offline (computed template answers, no LLM).
The service always responds with a tier field; honest degradation beats both silence and confident guessing.
The grounding guard extracts numbers from LLM answers (skipping timestamps, ids, clock times) and verifies each against tool payloads.
Labels: verified / unverified (with offending tokens listed) for LLM tiers; computed for offline answers.

offline

quiz.explain: Offline answers are templates filled from tool results — every figure comes straight from the data. There is no free-form generation step that could introduce unsupported numbers.

lessons.title: What is Physical AI
lessons.body_html:
AI that touches the world

Physical AI is artificial intelligence that senses the physical world, decides what to do, and acts back on it through motors, wheels, or grippers. A chatbot's worst-case output is a wrong sentence; a robot's worst-case output is a forklift-sized machine driving through a wall. That single difference — consequences are physical and irreversible — shapes everything about how the field works.

The loop every robot runs

Strip away the vendor branding and every autonomous machine runs the same pipeline, dozens of times per second:

  • Sensors — LiDAR, cameras, IMUs, wheel encoders produce raw measurements.
  • Perception — algorithms turn raw data into meaning: obstacles, people, pallets, free space.
  • State estimation — the robot fuses evidence into a belief about itself: where am I, how fast, how charged?
  • Planning — pick a goal and a route: which waypoint next, which task, which speed.
  • Control — convert the plan into precise motor commands hundreds of times per second.
  • Actuation — motors and brakes move the machine, changing the world, which the sensors then re-measure. The loop closes.

Watch any robot on the YantraFleet console map and you are watching this loop's output: the pos updates are state estimation, the route it follows is planning, the smooth motion between waypoints is control.

Why this is harder than software AI

Four properties make Physical AI a different sport:

  • Partial observability. Sensors are noisy and see only part of the scene. The robot never knows the world; it maintains a probabilistic belief — and beliefs can be wrong, which is exactly what happens when our simulated AMR-07 loses localization.
  • Real time. A language model may think for thirty seconds; a robot rolling at 1.2 m/s toward a person may not. Perception and control run on hard deadlines, often on small onboard computers.
  • Safety. Mistakes cost equipment and can injure people, so safety-rated hardware (scanner fields, e-stops) sits below the AI and overrides it.
  • The sim-to-real gap. Most training and testing happens in simulation because reality is slow and expensive — but simulators are never perfectly faithful, so behavior that works in sim can fail on the floor.

Embodiments: one loop, many bodies

The same loop wears different bodies. Fixed industrial arms weld and pick with sub-millimeter repeatability. AMRs (autonomous mobile robots, like this platform's simulated fleet) haul goods across warehouse floors. Humanoids aim at human-shaped spaces and tools and, as of 2026, are mostly in pilots rather than production. Drones run the loop in 3D under tight weight and power budgets. Autonomous vehicles run it at highway speed among the public — the hardest safety case of all. The economics differ wildly, but a perception bug or a bad state estimate looks remarkably similar in all of them, which is why the concepts in this track transfer across the whole industry.
key_points: Physical AI = AI that senses, decides, and acts in the physical world, where mistakes are irreversible.
Every robot runs the same loop: sensors → perception → state estimation → planning → control → actuation.
It is harder than software AI because of partial observability, hard real-time deadlines, safety stakes, and the sim-to-real gap.
A robot never knows the world — it maintains a belief, and wrong beliefs (like AMR-07's lost localization) are a routine failure class.
Embodiments differ — arms, AMRs, humanoids, drones, AVs — but the loop and its failure modes are shared.

quiz.q: Which ordering correctly describes the robot autonomy loop?
options: Planning → sensors → actuation → perception
Sensors → perception → state estimation → planning → control → actuation
Control → planning → sensors → state estimation
Perception → actuation → sensors → planning
quiz.explain: Raw sensor data is interpreted by perception, fused into a state estimate (where am I?), used to plan, executed by control, and finally actuated — which changes the world the sensors measure next. The loop repeats many times per second.

quiz.q: Why does a robot maintain a 'belief' about its position instead of simply knowing it?
options: Because GPS is illegal indoors
Because sensors are noisy and only partially observe the world, so position must be estimated probabilistically
Because robot vendors encrypt the true position
Because positions are only computed once at startup
quiz.explain: Partial observability is fundamental: every sensor is noisy and sees only part of the scene, so the robot fuses evidence into a probabilistic estimate. When the evidence stops matching the map, the belief degrades — that is a localization loss.

quiz.q: What most fundamentally separates Physical AI from a purely digital AI system?
options: It uses larger neural networks
It always runs in the cloud
Its outputs cause physical, irreversible effects under real-time and safety constraints
It cannot use machine learning
quiz.explain: A wrong token can be regenerated; a wrong motor command moves mass through space. Physical consequences plus hard deadlines plus safety stakes are what make the discipline different, not model size or hosting.

practical.instructions_html:
See the loop with your own eyes.

  • Start the platform (python -m yantraops up --loopback) and open the console map.
  • Pick one robot and follow it for two minutes. Identify each loop stage in what you observe: its pos updating (state estimation), the waypoint route it takes (planning), the smooth motion and speed changes (control), and the battery/motor readings (sensing).
  • Around sim tick 20, watch AMR-07: its localization belief fails and it stops doing useful work — a perception-layer failure propagating through the whole loop.

verify.prompt: For the robot you watched, name one observed behavior for each of: state estimation, planning, and control. What happened to AMR-07's loop when its localization belief failed?

lessons.tutor_context: Physical AI: AI that senses, decides, acts in the physical world; mistakes are irreversible. The autonomy loop (runs many times/second): sensors (LiDAR, cameras, IMU, wheel encoders) -> perception (raw data to meaning: obstacles, free space) -> state estimation (fused belief: pose, speed, battery) -> planning (goal + route/waypoints) -> control (motor commands, hundreds of Hz) -> actuation (motors move robot; world changes; sensors re-measure; loop closes). Harder than software AI: (1) partial observability — noisy, incomplete sensing; robot holds a probabilistic belief, not truth; (2) hard real-time deadlines on small onboard computers; (3) safety — safety-rated hardware (scanner fields, e-stop) sits below the AI and overrides it; (4) sim-to-real gap — trained/tested in simulation, sim is never perfectly faithful. Embodiments: industrial arms (fixed, sub-mm repeatability), AMRs (this platform's fleet: 10 simulated AMRs), humanoids (mostly pilots as of 2026), drones (3D, tight power budget), autonomous vehicles (hardest safety case).
